paper_sections.title: Interaction of schizophrenia and chronic cannabis use on reward anticipation sensitivity

description.value: The study examined how schizophrenia and chronic cannabis use interact to influence behavioural and neural sensitivity to reward anticipation.

design.value: A 2 × 2 factorial comparison of cannabis use and schizophrenia status was conducted in healthy controls and schizophrenia patients during a two-choice reward anticipation reaction-time task with functional MRI. Behavioural analyses used repeated-measures ANCOVA, and imaging analyses used first-level GLMs followed by ROI-based second-level validation and main analyses.

task_description.value: A two-choice RT task was used with elements of the MID and Eriksen flanker tasks. Participants responded to a series of five arrow heads with their right or left index finger according to the pointing direction of the central arrowhead. The task was completed during fMRI in one session and was divided into six blocks of 60 trials.

instructions.value: The aim of the task was to gain a maximal amount of points and in order for them to win (+) or avoid losing (−), they must respond both accurately and quickly.

stimuli.value: Only the incongruent configuration of five arrow heads was used (<<><< or >><>>). A valence cue, either + (win), − (lose) or * (neutral), was followed by a magnitude cue representing the amount of the upcoming reward: high 20, low 5, or none 0.

description.value: A high-resolution T1 anatomical image with 1 × 1 × 1 mm voxel size was acquired for each participant.

Raw images were spatially realigned, temporally interpolated to correct for delay in slice acquisition, normalized to standard Montreal Neurological Institute space and smoothed with an 8 mm full width at half maximum Gaussian kernel. Data with registered motion greater than 3 mm or 1 degree were excluded.

model_type.value: general linear model (GLM) and 2 × 2 × 5 analysis of covariance (ANCOVA)

model_settings.value: Reward condition was the within-subject repeated measures factor with five levels; cannabis use and schizophrenia were between-group fixed factors with two levels each; education level and age were continuous covariates.

Three contrast values for directional accuracy and three for mean reaction time were computed for each subject: valence, reward versus punishment, and magnitude. These contrast values were used as dependent variables in a GLM 2 × 2 ANCOVA with cannabis use and schizophrenia as fixed factors and years of education and age as continuous covariates.

A first-level within-subject GLM was applied separately to the valence and magnitude models. The valence model included three regressors, reward (+), punishment (−) and neutral (*). The magnitude model included five regressors, −20, −5, 0, +5 and +20. Motion correction parameters estimated from the realignment step were included as additional regressors. A high-pass filter with a 128 s cut-off was applied. T-contrasts were calculated for valence, reward versus punishment and magnitude.

A second-level validation ROI analysis was carried out with one-sample t-tests for each contrast. Analyses were restricted to predefined striatum, thalamus, amygdala and insula ROIs, with small volume correction and family-wise error correction at p < 0.05 within each independent ROI at the voxel level; a minimum cluster size of three contiguous voxels was used.

estimator.value: Gaussian random field theory for small volume correction

model_settings.value: The main analysis assessed modulation of each contrast by cannabis use, schizophrenia status and their interaction, with years of education and age as covariates. The analysis was restricted to the predefined ROIs and used family-wise error correction adjusted for small volume at p < 0.05, with a minimum cluster size of three contiguous voxels.
